summary.text: The Euclidean algorithm is an efficient method for finding the greatest common divisor of two integers, the largest number that divides both without a remainder.
It rests on the fact that the greatest common divisor stays the same when the larger number is replaced by its difference with the smaller, repeated until the two numbers are equal.
One of the oldest algorithms in common use, it reduces fractions to simplest form and sits inside the cryptography that secures internet communications.

facts.label: Named after
facts.value: Euclid, who described it around 300 BC

facts.label: Worked example
facts.value: 21 is the GCD of 252 and 105, as 252 = 21 × 12

facts.label: Remainder shortcut
facts.value: Steps never exceed five times the smaller number's digits

facts.label: Lamé's proof
facts.value: Gabriel Lamé proved that step limit in 1844

facts.label: Bézout link
facts.value: The GCD can be written as a combination, e.g. 21 = 5 × 105 + (−2) × 252

items.prompt: You are hunting for the biggest number dividing both 252 and 105, and you replace 252 with 252 − 105 = 147. What happens to the answer?

options.label: It stays the same, since 105 and 147 share the same biggest divisor
It doubles, because the larger number got smaller
It becomes 147, the new larger number
It must be started again from the beginning

items.explain: The greatest common divisor does not change when the larger number is replaced by its difference with the smaller one.

items.prompt: You keep replacing the larger of two numbers by its difference with the smaller until both numbers are the same. What is that final number?

options.label: The product of the original two
The greatest common divisor of the original two
The smaller of the original two
The sum of the original two

items.explain: Each replacement keeps the GCD unchanged, so when the numbers match, that number is the GCD.

items.prompt: One number is huge and the other is tiny, so repeated subtraction would take thousands of steps. What shortcut does the improved version use?

options.label: Add the two numbers together instead of subtracting
Halve the huge number again and again each time
Swap the larger for its remainder after dividing by the smaller
Break both numbers into primes before doing anything

items.explain: Replacing the larger number by its remainder after division by the smaller bundles many subtractions into one step.

items.prompt: You need the common divisor of two enormous numbers. What is the main advantage of Euclid's method over factoring each number first?

options.label: It hands you both numbers' prime factors as a bonus
It only works when each number is itself a prime
It guesses an answer and then checks it much later
It skips prime factors, which are very hard to find when large

items.explain: Factoring large integers is believed to be very difficult, and the Euclidean algorithm avoids it.

items.prompt: Neither 6 nor 35 is a prime number. Can they still be coprime?

options.label: Yes, their only shared factor is 1
No, coprime numbers must each be prime
No, any two numbers share a factor larger than 1
Yes, but only because one of them is odd

items.explain: Coprime means the GCD is 1. With 6 = 2 × 3 and 35 = 5 × 7, they have no common prime factors.

items.prompt: You want to cover a 24×60 floor with identical square tiles, with no cutting. What is the largest tile side that works?
items.explain: The largest square side that fits both edges exactly is the GCD of 24 and 60, which is 12 (24/12 = 2 and 60/12 = 5).

paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: The Euclidean algorithm is an efficient method for finding the greatest common divisor, or GCD, of two integers: the largest number that divides both of them with no remainder. Its name comes from Euclid, a mathematician of ancient Greece, who was the first to describe it, in his Elements around 300 BC. It is one of the oldest algorithms still in common use.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: It is used to reduce fractions to their simplest form and to carry out division in modular arithmetic. A key advantage is that it finds the GCD without first working out the prime factors of the numbers. Factoring large integers is believed to be very hard, and the security of many widely used cryptographic protocols depends on that. Calculations with the algorithm are part of the protocols that secure internet communications.

paragraphs.heading: How it works
paragraphs.text: The method rests on one fact: the GCD of two numbers does not change if you replace the larger one by the difference between them. For 252 and 105 the GCD is 21, and 21 is also the GCD of 105 and 147, which is 252 − 105. Each replacement shrinks the larger number, so repeating it gives smaller and smaller pairs until the two numbers are equal. That number is the GCD of the original pair.

paragraphs.heading: A faster version
paragraphs.text: Euclid's original subtraction version can take many steps when one number is much bigger than the other. A faster version replaces the larger number by its remainder after dividing by the smaller one, and stops when the remainder reaches zero. Done this way, the number of steps is never more than five times the number of base-10 digits in the smaller integer. Gabriel Lamé proved this in 1844, and his result marks the beginning of computational complexity theory.

paragraphs.heading: Writing the GCD as a sum
paragraphs.text: Running the steps backwards, or using the extended Euclidean algorithm, writes the GCD as the two original numbers, each times some integer, added together. For example, 21 = 5 × 105 + (−2) × 252. The fact that the GCD can always be written this way is called Bézout's identity.

paragraphs.heading: A picture of the GCD
paragraphs.text: Picture a rectangle a by b, and a number c that divides both sides exactly. You can then cut the sides into pieces of length c, splitting the rectangle into a grid of c by c squares. The GCD is the largest c for which this works. A 24 by 60 rectangle can be tiled with squares of side 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 or 12, so the GCD of 24 and 60 is 12.

paragraphs.heading: Further uses
paragraphs.text: The algorithm also helps solve Diophantine equations, build continued fractions, and find accurate fraction approximations to real numbers. It is a basic tool in proofs, for example of Lagrange's four-square theorem and of the fact that prime factorizations are unique. Euclid described it only for natural numbers and geometric lengths, but in the 19th century it was extended to Gaussian integers and polynomials of one variable. That led to modern ideas in abstract algebra such as Euclidean domains.
